title: How do I grab all parameters from a URL and print it out in PHP?
author: Stefan Bogdanescu

content:
# Iterating Over URL Parameters in PHP When you receive a request with a long list of query string arguments, manually accessing them via `$_GET['param']` quickly becomes impractical. This approach forces you to know every key beforehand and requires repetitive code for every single parameter. The standard solution is to treat the `$_GET` superglobal as an associative array and iterate over it using a loop. To print all parameters and their values, you simply need to access the keys of the array. PHP provides several built-in functions that make this straightforward without requiring external libraries. The most common approach involves using `array_keys()` combined with `foreach`, or iterating directly if you only care about the key-value pairs as they appear in the request. Consider a URL like `https://example.com/search?query=php&limit=10&sort=date`. When this hits your server, PHP populates the `$_GET` array with keys `query`, `limit`, and `sort`. You can traverse this collection using a simple loop: ```php foreach ($_GET as $key => $value) { echo htmlspecialchars($key) . ' = ' . htmlspecialchars($value) . "
"; } ``` This snippet outputs every parameter in the format `key = value`. Notice the use of `htmlspecialchars()`. This is critical for security. If a user injects malicious HTML or JavaScript into a query parameter, echoing it directly to the browser without encoding can lead to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities. Encoding ensures that special characters are displayed safely as text rather than executed code. You might also encounter scenarios where you need to check for specific keys first before iterating, perhaps to handle default values. In those cases, `isset()` or the null coalescing operator can help manage missing parameters gracefully. However, if your goal is strictly to dump everything present in the URL string, iterating over `$_GET` covers all GET variables passed via the query string. What about POST data? If the form submission method was `POST`, those values reside in `$_POST`. The logic for iteration remains identical: ```php foreach ($_POST as $key => $value) { // handle post data } ``` However, there is a nuance with file uploads. Files sent via POST do not appear in `$_POST` or `$_GET` because they are binary streams. Accessing them requires using the `$_FILES` superglobal, which contains metadata about each uploaded file rather than the file content itself. Mixing these sources can lead to confusion if you expect a single array to hold all request data. Additionally, be aware of how PHP handles multiple values for the same key. If a URL contains `?user=alice&user=bob`, PHP treats this as an array where the key maps to a list of values: `['alice', 'bob']`. When iterating with `foreach`, you will see the key repeated, and each iteration will yield one value from that list. This behavior is consistent across most modern PHP versions (5.4+), but older versions might behave differently depending on configuration. If you are working within a Laravel application, handling query strings often involves accessing the `request` instance instead of directly manipulating superglobals. While direct access to `$_GET` works in raw PHP scripts, using the framework's request object provides better abstraction and security features out of the box. The underlying mechanism remains iterating over an array, but the entry point is cleaner. For more details on handling requests efficiently in Laravel, you can refer to resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com). Ultimately, iterating over `$_GET` or `$_POST` using a loop is the most efficient way to process all parameters dynamically. It avoids hardcoding keys and scales regardless of how many arguments are passed in the URL.
